newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks tax dialogue with unions, church.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks tax dialogue with unions, church.

text.p: Amid mounting criticism of a government tax plan unveiled earlier this week, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday dismissed allegations from churches, trade unions and opposition parties it was unfair.

The government approved a tax reform this week that lowers basic tax rates, resulting in tax cuts of 82 billion marks ($50.04 billion), which would be partially offset by cutting tax breaks and raising value-added taxes.
In the end, German taxpayers should be given a net reduction in income taxes of 30 billion marks from 1999.

But no sooner had the plan been presented to the public than a barrage of criticism poured in from trade unions, opposition parties and the church, who for various reasons saw the tax cuts helping a wealthy few while hitting the many poor.

Speaking at a meeting of his Christian Democrat (CDU) party in Hesse state, Kohl defended the government's plan to cut income taxes and reduce the solidarity tax -- a surcharge on income tax bills to finance rebuilding east Germany.
He called on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens to present alternatives.
"But first you have to come up with a net reduction of 30 billion marks plus 7.5 billion marks from cutting the solidarity tax," Kohl told party members.
Commenting on criticism from church circles, he said he hoped that religious leaders had more to say than "just that their 10 percent of tax revenues is not enough".
Ahead of next week's presentation of plans for a reform of the pension payment system, Kohl defended the government's intention to raise taxes on pension payments.
"If a businessman pays 4,000 marks on annual income of 36,000 and a pensioner just 190 marks, then we have to create a more just system," he said.

Kohl reiterated that it was necessary to revamp the pension system because life expectancy and the retirement age were no longer in line. He said although average life expectancy was 76 years, Germans worked an average 30 years.

"Whoever fails to admit this is lying to the people and you cannot change that by blowing a whistle," he said in a reference to loud protests by several hundred members of the DGB trade union federation.
